unmapped_findings: Atomic sizes of the elements in the steels (Table 5 / Fig. 18): Fe 124 pm, Mn 124 pm, Al 143 pm, Be 111 pm, C 77 pm; Mn, Al and Be form substitution solid solutions while C forms an interstitial solid solution.

Lattice-distortion behaviour relevant to the 1.0Be steel: the Be atom (111 pm) is smaller than Fe (124 pm) so it causes inward lattice shrinkage, whereas Al (143 pm) causes outward lattice expansion; although Be density is low (1.87 g/cm³), its inward lattice distortion means Be does not have a strong lightweighting effect on the density.

Per the Fe–Be binary phase diagram, essentially no Be is soluble in austenite (Be solubility in austenite <1%) and Be precipitates as compounds once the austenite is saturated, whereas ferrite can dissolve much larger amounts of Be; this explains the Be–Fe phase distribution (the 1.0Be rolled steel dissolves more Be in the ferrite, reducing precipitate content relative to 1.5Be).

After hot deformation the as-cast needle-like (ancient Chinese character shaped) Be–Fe phase in the 1.0Be steel is transformed into spherical and point shapes, most Be being solubilised into the matrix, which reduces the precipitate content.

DSC of the 1.0Be alloy shows a phase transformation peak at 1163.3 °C (after homogenisation, heating at 10 °C/min); Be addition shifts the transformation temperature of the alloy down by roughly 120 °C relative to the Be-free steel.
